x.text:
A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible.

The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK:

- Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes
- Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them
- Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code to check if it's really dead and if so, remove it the next day
- Abstraction police: fixes leaky abstractions
- a bunch more..

Results have been surprisingly positive. Over the last few weeks, these routines have opened 388 PRs across our repos, 180 of which we merged after Claude Code Review + human review. We're now thinking about how to streamline this to make merging these kinds of mechanical changes easier.

Claude generally gets these PRs right on the first shot, and if it doesn't, we ask Claude to tune its routines so it's better the next day. Sometimes it takes a few days of tuning. 

To try a similar workflow, ask Claude Code or Tag, or create some routines directly at https://t.co/Z70hStEBH6. A few of the actual prompts I used below.

Has anyone experimented with similar workflows?

Prompt debt is the new tech debt. 

With every model update, you should be cutting at least 50% of your prompts.

Most AI products have bloated prompts that are making your product quality worse.

The typical flow is: model fails at something -> add 10 rules. Tool call fails -> add 10 examples. Output is weird -> add formatting constraints.

3 months later, your system prompt is a novel. 

Meanwhile the model is way smarter and your micro-managey prompts are turning it into a dumb rules machine.

The elimination of engineers was one of the wilder hypotheses out there. Just like absurdly wrong. We just gave engineers a power tool that can accelerate the development of whatever we want. 

Of course their value not only remains critical in that world, but actually goes up in many domains because we can apply engineering to far more work than before.

If you’re trying to automate drug discovery, you need engineers. If you’re trying to automate manufacturing, you need engineers. If you’re taking on larger and larger software projects, you need engineers.

This will happen in domains beyond engineering too. AI causes companies to take on way more work than before, which leads to needing more experts to oversee the work. 

Even as models get better and better, they can be better utilized by the experts in those fields than the novices. Great time to be an expert.

x.text:
Grok Bot is a fantastic release.. the UX, the design, the onboarding :chefs-kiss:

But I go back and forth on this a lot: Will users (personal and business) want one super agent that holds all the context or sub agents that are designated to do a slice of tasks?

If we treat agents as humans, then the Grok Bot design makes a ton of sense. It allows us to compartmentalize tools, context, outcomes for that person’s division. You reach out to that bot for that specific goal that you have in mind. 

But, if you treat agents as Jarvis, you want a master agent that just gets the job done. It might create and coordinate all the bots (and dare I say the communication/context) that might be needed to do the task. But the interface is 1:1 vs. 1:many. 

My guess is it’ll veer towards the one master agent over time who can then act as an orchestrator who reads / understands the bots you create. But starts narrow as most of the companies are doing it now. 

PS: I understand the core engineering constraints (context windows, tool use, simplicity, cost etc) why companies are choosing task/singular outcomes today. Primarily thinking this from a design / product side.

podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: What Chess.com Teaches US About Superhuman Capabilities, with CEO Erik Allebest
podcasts.transcript:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:24
COVID happened, Queen's Gambit happened, some news cycles happened, and we're like, oh, this might just be a flash in the pan, like treadmills and sourdough bread. But then in 2023, we had another crazy wave where all these kids started playing in schools because of short form content and the mittens bot and the cheating scandal. And we just spiked again. And then when we came down again, we were so much higher and we maintained this baseline.

Speaker 2 | 00:24 - 00:29
How do you think about, like, how to design a rating system for poker?

Speaker 1 | 00:29 - 00:48
We're bringing the chess playbook, which is like, how good are you really? Not just can you buy the most chips or can you use a bot or can you steal the most money? Whatever it is, we've all played those games where you're playing for M and M's and someone's just, like, all in all the time and they just rebuy more M and M's. As people get used to, like, wait. I actually care about my poker rating.

Speaker 1 | 00:48 - 00:57
People are gonna care about it as much as money because it's a reflection of, like, the value and their skill as a player. I think this is gonna be quite an interesting innovation for for

Speaker 2 | 01:10 - 01:44
the chess.com domain out of bankruptcy auction in 2005 for $55 when almost every investor told him it was an uninvestable niche passion project. Two decades later, he's built the dominant chess platform with more than 250,000,000 members, 200,000,000 a year in revenue and a mission to get a billion people to play chess. It's a game that's more popular than ever, despite computers outclassing humans at it for the last thirty years. We talk about what AI means for games, the future of chess.com, how to build a rating system for poker and the future of human skills. Welcome, Eric.

Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:47
Eric, it's great to have you on No Priors. Welcome.

Speaker 1 | 01:47 - 01:49
Thank you so much for having me.

Speaker 2 | 01:49 - 02:05
So I'd love to just make sure our listeners have a little bit of the backstory of chess.com and how you built this business. But could you paint a little bit of a picture of just, you know, usage and both the company and the user base and product today first?

Speaker 1 | 02:05 - 02:25
Yeah, sure. We are we are much larger than I ever thought we would be. So it's kind of wild to say these numbers for me. We're about 10,000,000 daily active users, about 40 or 50,000,000 monthly active users. It's always a little slower in the summertime as people are, you know, in the, in the Northern Hemisphere out and about.

Speaker 1 | 02:26 - 02:55
We have more than two fifty million registered members and more revenue than I thought we would end up with as a chess company. A little, I think this year we'll do a little over 200,000,000, which is frankly, again, surprising. We have about six fifty people on our team who love chess, are passionate about the game, and are working hard to, you know, make our members happy and to grow the game, and to be the best possible place to work. Those are our three kind of the three areas of our mission.

Speaker 2 | 02:55 - 03:10
Amazing. And you took a, I guess, somewhat unconventional startup path or founder CEO path to get here. I'm certainly think of you as founder. What how did you end up owning the business?

Speaker 1 | 03:11 - 03:41
Well, we didn't start by owning a business. We just started by owning a domain name that we got from a bankruptcy auction in 2005. Someone else owned the domain name. They were building chess software, but they, you know, couldn't pay their, their debts and, and the money they'd raised a little bit of money to try to do that, and ended up with a failed business. And so, a friend and I bought the chess.com domain name for $56,000 and we were going to build a chess community.

Speaker 1 | 03:41 - 03:53
We wanted to be like MySpace and build a chess community where people could kind of come and, and and express themselves and learn and share. We bought the domain name and started building.

Speaker 2 | 03:53 - 04:00
And, we'll bridge the gap from that to the scale of community you have today. Like, how did you grow? How did you think about fundraising?

Speaker 1 | 04:01 - 04:16

podcasts.summaryZh: 本期《No Priors》对话 Chess.com CEO Erik Allebest，围绕 Chess.com 如何从一个'不可投资'的小众项目成长为行业主导者，以及 AI 对棋类/游戏和人类技能的影响展开。Chess.com 于 2005 年以 5.6 万美元拍得域名起步，当时几乎所有风投都劝他别投，于是他自筹资金'按现金速度'增长、从不融资，如今拥有 2.5 亿会员、年收入超 2 亿美元、650 人团队，使命是让十亿人下棋。文化层面，借助《后翼弃兵》、短视频、'Mittens'机器人和作弊丑闻等契机，平台重新定义了'会下棋的人'——不再以 2000+ 评级为门槛，人人都是棋手。关于 AI，Allebest 认为超级智能并未让棋变无聊，反而通过引擎、AI 教练和谜题生成让人类学得更快、玩得更投入，人类仍渴望'人的活动'。他强调掌握技能没有捷径，靠重复练习，把每天做的事乘以一千，习惯会随时间复利增长。护城河方面，棋类无法专利，最终靠体验、内容和社区取胜；平台还推出扑克产品 Gambit，把'建立评级体系'的象棋方法论迁移到扑克。最后他对 AGI 持谨慎乐观态度，认为风险更多是文化问题而非技术问题，呼吁设立护栏。
